questions.stem: What is the primary unit of design in Event-Driven Data Modelling?
options: The event, a discrete occurrence capturing something that has happened
The static entity such as Customer or Loan
questions.explanation: Event-driven modelling treats events, each representing a fact in time with a timestamp and contextual details, as the primary unit of design rather than static entities.

questions.stem: What two properties characterise events in an event-driven model?
questions.explanation: Events are immutable and append-only: once an event is written it is never updated or deleted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example event from the loan approval domain?
questions.explanation: Typical loan approval events include LoanApplicationSubmitted, LoanApplicationApproved and RepaymentMade, each with identifying information, context and a timestamp.

questions.stem: How is the current state of a loan determined in an event-driven system?
options: It is stored directly in a Loan table
It is cached in a key–value store as the source of truth
It is looked up from a dimension table
It is derived by replaying the sequence of events
It is computed by joining fact and dimension tables
questions.explanation: Because events are preserved in sequence, the state of the system can be reconstructed at any point in time by replaying the event log; the current state is derived, not stored.

questions.stem: Which platform is named as an event streaming implementation for a loan approval system?
questions.explanation: A bank might implement an event streaming platform such as Apache Kafka, with Pulsar and Kinesis also named as distributed streaming platforms.

questions.stem: In the event-driven loan example, what happens after the underwriting service consumes a LoanApplicationSubmitted event?
options: It processes the application and emits a LoanApplicationApproved or LoanApplicationRejected event
It updates the original event with the decision
It writes the decision to a dimension table
questions.explanation: The underwriting service consumes the submitted event, processes it and emits a new approved or rejected event; the original event is never modified.

questions.stem: Which teams can subscribe to the same loan event streams in real time without interfering with operational systems?
options: Fraud detection, compliance monitoring and analytics teams
questions.explanation: Fraud detection, compliance monitoring and analytics teams can subscribe to the same streams in real time without disturbing operational processing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of event-driven data modelling?
options: A built-in audit trail because every change is an immutable event
Simple infrastructure with no need for streaming platforms
Replayability to rebuild projections or generate analytics retrospectively
Support for audit, compliance, debugging, simulation and machine learning training
questions.explanation: Event-driven systems typically require distributed streaming platforms such as Kafka, Pulsar or Kinesis, and event replay needs careful infrastructure support; simplicity is not a strength.

questions.stem: Which challenge is named as part of the complexity of event-driven modelling?
options: Managing event schema versioning rigorously as systems evolve
questions.explanation: Event schema versioning must be managed rigorously, alongside designing idempotent consumers and ensuring consistency across services.

questions.stem: Why do normalisation forms not directly apply to event-driven modelling?
options: Because events are always stored in 6NF
Because events are stored as graph edges
Because event stores enforce domain–key constraints
Because events are append-only records centred on temporal sequencing rather than relational dependency theory
questions.explanation: Events are append-only records that may follow schema-on-write or schema-on-read patterns, and the design centres on temporal sequencing rather than functional dependencies.
